item.title: Sports club members becoming less tolerant of homosexuality
item.description:
Sports club members becoming less tolerant of homosexuality

October 27, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Acceptance of homosexuality in Dutch sports clubs has declined significantly in the last generation, according to a survey of attitudes by the Mulier Institute.

The organisation found that 66% of people had no objection to a fellow member of a sports club being gay, while in 2008 the figure was 85%.

Just over half (55%) of respondents said they had no problem sharing a shower with a gay team-mate of the same sex, which also represented a drop from 73% in 2008.

The Mulier Institute said the findings reflected a social trend that has also been seen in schools, where the proportion of boys aged between 12 and 16 with a positive view of homosexuality has dropped from 40% to 22% since 2021.

The Dutch Olympic Committee NOC*NSF said the findings were “highly regrettable” and pledged to step up its efforts to make sport more inclusive.

But the John Blankenstein Foundation, which campaigns for LGBT emancipation in sport, said it had noticed declining enthusiasm for its workshops and growing numbers of parents who voiced objections.

Karin Blankenstein, who set up the organisation in 2008, told NOS: “I get the sensitivity around transgender people in sport at the top level, but this is about amateur sport.”

item.title: Beekse Bergen zookeeper dies after leopard attack
item.description:
Beekse Bergen zookeeper dies after leopard attack

October 27, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

A zookeeper at Beekse Bergen safari park has succumbed to her injuries after being attacked by a leopard in one of the park’s enclosures on Saturday.

The woman, who had spent nearly 40 years working with the animals, was said to be a highly committed and experienced member of the park.

Two male Persian panthers, a type of leopard, had taken shelter in an enclosure in the park amid stormy weather over the weekend. It is unclear how or why they attacked the keeper as there is no CCTV footage and entering an indoor enclosure with the animals is highly unusual.

She managed to call for help via a walkie-talkie during the attack but was mauled badly on her head and neck.

Emergency workers, including an air ambulance, rushed to the scene. Her injuries were so serious that officials at the park said it was unlikely she would survive.

An investigation into the accident has been launched by the labour inspectorate.

item.title: Rare “angel of death” mushroom found growing in Soest
item.description:
Rare “angel of death” mushroom found growing in Soest

October 27, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

An extremely rare poisonous mushroom known as the “angel of death”, or formally Amanita virosa, has been discovered growing in Soest, a town in the Utrecht countryside.

It is considered a “notorious” species of fungus among mycologists, according to RTV Utrecht, for its toxicity and rarity. It was presumed extinct in the region and is designated as endangered.

Mycologist Rob Chrispijn told RTV he “jumped for joy” when he found one growing while leading a tour of the De Paltz estate in Soest. The species’ decline has come amid increased acidity in the soil, something related to the nitrogen crisis.

The fungus can be easily mistaken for an edible button mushroom, but failing to distinguish it before picking and eating could be life-threatening.

Chrispijn said that symptoms wouldn’t be immediate, but later you could suffer severe gastrointestinal problems and nausea after digesting, and “after two days, the liver and kidneys are affected, and the consequences can be permanent.”

Only two of the mushrooms were found on the estate, one of which is being examined for research. The other is remaining in the ground where it was, but Chrispijn said he isn’t worried anyone will be careless enough to eat it.

item.title: Education minister threatens to pull funding from Islamic school
item.description:
Education minister threatens to pull funding from Islamic school

October 27, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Junior education minister Judith Tielen has threatened to withdraw funding from an Islamic secondary school in Amsterdam unless it drastically improves exam performance.

The Cornelius Haga Lyceum has been told to appoint two extra board members, draw up a plan for improvements and send a progress report to the ministry every four weeks.

Tielen said it was “unacceptable that these pupils receive a substandard education every day” after inspectors found that their results were lagging behind children in other schools.

“School should be a place where children can develop and make progress,” Tielen said. “School administrators have a responsibility to make sure of that.”

Inspectors concluded in July that the Islamic Education Foundation (SIO), which runs the school, was guilty of mismanagement and the quality of education on offer was below acceptable standards.

In the last three years only 35% of students at the mavo level, a vocational stream, passed their exams, against a national average of 91%.

Wouter Pors, the lawyer for the school, told NOS that the board accepted the need for improvements, but the government was partly responsible for the problems.

“It is difficult for all schools to find qualified teachers, but for the Haga Lyceum it is even harder in practice. Applicants for secondary roles regularly withdraw, which leads to high numbers of lessons being cancelled.”

item.title: Fatal Rotterdam explosion suspect acquitted for lack of evidence
item.description:
Fatal Rotterdam explosion suspect acquitted for lack of evidence

October 27, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

A man suspected of causing an explosion in Rotterdam two years ago, in which three people died, has been acquitted.

Jalal O., a 37-year-old man who rented a garage in the Schammenkamp area of the city, was accused of using the premises as a drugs lab for processing cocaine.

In the aftermath of the explosion he climbed through the rubble looking for victims, and was initially perceived by local residents as a “hero”, according to media reports.

The explosion tore through the apartment complex above it, spreading a fire and partially collapsing the building. Besides the three who died, several were seriously injured and some lost their homes permanently.

After investigators analysed the scene, they found evidence including more than 40 acetone containers, traces of cocaine and procaine, and other paraphernalia. Prosecutors also found app messages between O. and his nephew they said were related to drug dealing.

In a procedural hearing after O.’s arrest in 2024, it was also disclosed that he had a previous conviction for drugs offences in Spain. He has always maintained his innocence and said at the time he had never been involved in the drug trade.

Prosecutors sought a seven-year sentence. If he had been convicted, the surviving victims would also have been eligible for compensation. They could instead take out a civil case against O. now that he has been acquitted.

The court found there was not enough evidence to convict him, and found no proof that the premises had been used as a drugs lab. It noted that the exact reason for the explosion remains unknown.

O. was a tenant of the garage but had sublet the space, and the court said the prosecution could not prove beyond a reasonable doubt that he was responsible.

item.title: How to balance a career and a master’s in the Netherlands
item.description:
Partner content

How to balance a career and a master’s in the Netherlands

October 27, 2026

Working full time while studying for a master’s can be a tough balancing act. Melina Gkiolma, a sustainability consultant and currently a student on the Online Master Sustainability Management at Rotterdam School of Management, Erasmus University (RSM) in Amsterdam, talks about how she handles the burden.

For many internationals in the Netherlands, going back to university means fitting lectures and assignments around a full-time job, family commitments and trips back home. Finding the time and the energy is often the biggest hurdle.

Melina, who is originally from Athens, has worked in the sustainability sector for five years, having spent the past 2.5 years as a sustainability consultant at Kōan, a boutique consultancy in Amsterdam. She started her career at Deloitte Luxembourg. She helps organisations deal with sustainability reporting requirements and changing regulations across Europe and beyond.

She wanted a part-time course she could follow online, so she could keep working while building her academic background in a field where she sees her long-term career. “This programme seemed like the perfect fit because it met all the criteria I was looking for,” she said.

Finding a routine
Returning to study took some adjustment. “I admit that returning to academic study after several years in the workplace was a little challenging at first,” she said, “but I’ve found a balance that works for me.”

She tries to join the live class every week and usually studies in the evening after work, when she is “already in a productive mindset”. She also puts in some time at weekends, but makes a point of keeping time free to relax.

Weekly updates from the programme managers on upcoming activities and assignment deadlines help her stay on top of the workload, she said.

Studying on the move
Because the course is entirely online, Melina can keep studying wherever she is – at home, on work trips or visiting her family in Greece.

She also found it more sociable than she expected. “People often assume online learning can feel impersonal, but my experience has been the opposite,” she said. Live classes, discussion forums and informal virtual coffee chats have helped her build strong ties with classmates around the world.

The international mix is one of her favourite parts of the course, with students from almost every continent. “It’s eye-opening to hear about people’s different experiences depending on where they live and their different professional backgrounds,” she said.

Theory into practice
Melina has been able to use what she learns at work straight away. Earlier in the programme, students were asked to develop key performance indicators (KPIs) for a logistics company. When a new client later asked her for help setting KPIs for its carbon emissions, she drew on the research she had done for that assignment.

“The master’s has also helped me broaden my horizons in sustainability. Because I work in sustainability reporting, there are many topics I hadn’t explored in depth before. One module I found particularly interesting focused on ethics and leadership. It made me reflect on what I want to stand for in my work, my moral compass, and the purpose behind the things I do. It really got me thinking.”

“Be kind to yourself”
Her advice to anyone thinking of combining a job with a part-time master’s is to go easy on themselves. “Working full time while studying for a part-time master is a significant challenge, but you can find the balance that works for you,” she said.
“And remember, pursuing further education while advancing your career is a major achievement in itself.”

Applications for the Online Master in Sustainability Management at RSM are now open for cohorts starting in 2027. Find out more about the programme and apply here.

item.title: The dual nationality dilemma: what Dutch News readers say
item.description:
The dual nationality dilemma: what Dutch News readers say

October 27, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Earlier this month we asked Dutch News’ readers for their thoughts on taking Dutch nationality, given that in many cases they would have to give up their original passport.

Legislation due to be discussed in parliament in early December should change that, but it now seems likely that foreigners will be excluded from the new rules – which will then only apply to the native Dutch who take on a second nationality.

The rules on dual nationality are complex and discriminatory. If you are married it is easier to become Dutch and retain your original passport, for example. It also gets easier once you reach the age of 65. But many readers are caught up in the complexity of the current “naturalisation” process. They want to become Dutch, but giving up their original nationality will create a new range of problems.

Over 80 readers told us their stories. Here is a selection of their experiences.

An impossible choice
“What I find difficult is that many people who have lived, worked, and contributed to Dutch society for years are forced to make a choice that other Dutch citizens are not required to make. I would gladly embrace Dutch citizenship, but not at the cost of losing an important part of my identity and connection to my family and heritage.” Ahmed, from Egypt

Bureaucratic nightmare
“I’m Chilean and have been living in the Netherlands for around 10 years. A few years ago, I decided to become Dutch. The Dutch naturalisation process itself was clear and straightforward for me. What I could never have imagined was the nightmare I would face in Chile afterwards.

“Renouncing Chilean nationality is effectively irreversible. Once you give it up, you cannot simply apply to get it back …The renunciation brought very serious practical consequences that I was not prepared for. My Chilean nationality was removed and I was deleted from Chile’s national registry.

“This means that I can no longer obtain basic documents such as a birth certificate in the normal way, despite having been born in Chile. Every time I need to deal with something in Chile, including matters concerning my own family and inheritance, I find myself unable to prove that I am the person who appears in their records. I have no Chilean identity documents anymore, and because I have been removed from the registry, I simply no longer exist in the country where I was born.

“The Dutch government describes the renunciation as something you do ‘voluntarily’. But I struggle with that description. If acquiring Dutch nationality means that I have to give up my original nationality in order to become Dutch, how voluntary is that choice really?” Jonathan, from Chile 

An easy decision
“I have lived here for 32 years – over half my life. I was born in Ireland but moved here in 1994. My wife is Dutch-born, our kids were born here and my life is here. I became a Dutch citizen about 15 years ago and gave up my Irish citizenship. I regard myself as culturally more Dutch now than Irish and choosing for a single nationality was a very easy decision.” Jim, from Ireland

Global freedom
“My wife loves it here, I’ve passed my inburgering exams, love my job, and contribute over €100k annually in taxes. But despite loving our life here, we’ve decided to leave soon. With the 30% ruling ending for me and the Netherlands requiring naturalising citizens to renounce their original nationality, staying no longer makes sense. My original passport represents my roots, family, and identity – I will never give it up.

“However, I do want the global freedom and security of a second passport. We’ve made the hard decision to move to Canada or the UK, where we can naturalise in five years or less without dropping our original nationality. It’s a sad move for my wife and a tough choice for both of us, but the current legal framework leaves high-contributing expats with very few practical alternatives.”  John, from Jordan

Where to retire?
“I have lived in Europe since 2001 and moved to Amsterdam in 2018 as I wanted to remain in Europe. As I am coming into the end of my career we are contemplating where we want to retire but have no mobility as our permanent residence is tied solely to the Netherlands.

“Right now, given the political situation in Canada, it pains me to surrender my nationality as I am a proud Canadian, but I must contemplate our future as a family that wishes to remain in Europe with the option to reside in a sunnier climate. It is also a shame given the long history between Canada and the Netherlands and the increasing closeness of Canada to the EU. After 25 years in Europe I am firmly European, but it feels unfair to force me to deny that I am also Canadian.” Adele, from Canada

Discrimination
“As I am not married, I am not able to apply for Dutch citizenship without renouncing my Australian citizenship. I find this quite disappointing and even discriminatory, given that, if I had a partner or spouse, I’d be allowed to have both. For that reason I have remained an Aussie, even though I’m not planning on moving back to there anytime soon.” James has lived in the Netherlands for more than 20 years.

Sister separation
“I have given up my nationality (British) and am now Dutch. The complete irony is I’m an identical twin so now I’m an identical twin where my sister has a different nationality. After Brexit I worry about how that may impact us when we are 80 and are less able to travel.” Tina, from Britain

Rise of the far right
“I declined on three occasions an invitation to attend the naturalisation ceremony because I found it difficult to give up my Filipino citizenship. The Philippines allows dual nationality while the Netherlands requires full allegiance.

“In the end, I had to make what felt like a very hard decision of renouncing my Filipino citizenship because PVV was the biggest party at the time. I was worried that living in the Netherlands would be difficult on account of the radical right leaning becoming the biggest political party.”  Brian, from the Philippines

Family ties
“I would love to apply for Dutch nationality, but because I still have family in the US, including an adult child and aging parents, I cannot give up my American passport.

“Sometimes the US does not allow people who have relinquished their passports to return, because they are considered a greater risk for overstaying their visas when compared to other visitors. I cannot risk being unable to visit my family, so I am applying for permanent residency instead of a Dutch passport.” Rick, from the US

Practical reasons
“I come from another EU country, and for me there is currently no possibility of becoming a Dutch citizen without renouncing my original nationality. As someone from a small country, this is not an easy decision. It is difficult not only for emotional reasons, but also for practical ones.

“I was born and raised in my country of origin, and my entire family still lives there. My nationality is therefore more than just a passport or a legal status; it is an important part of my identity and my connection to my family and where I come from.

“At the same time, my children were born and raised here in the Netherlands. They speak Dutch, attend Dutch schools, and grow up with Dutch traditions and culture. The Netherlands is their home. Yet, despite being fully part of Dutch society, they are not Dutch citizens and therefore cannot enjoy all the rights that come with citizenship, most notably the right to vote in national elections.

“This creates a difficult situation for families like mine. We can be deeply integrated into Dutch society and consider the Netherlands our home, while still facing a choice between retaining the nationality we were born with and becoming Dutch citizens.

“For me, this is not about rejecting my country of origin or refusing to become part of Dutch society. It is about wanting to preserve both parts of my identity and, at the same time, fully belong to the country where my children are growing up.” Anon

Some names have been changed to protect the privacy of the individuals concerned.

Our thanks to everyone who got in touch, and we will be contacting more of you in the coming period.

If you would like to comment on this article, or have any additional thoughts, don’t hesitate to get in touch via editor@dutchnews.nl. We will be publishing a series of articles focusing on dual nationality in the coming months.

item.title: Netherlands to stay away from Eurovision Song Contest after all
item.description:
Netherlands to stay away from Eurovision Song Contest after all

October 27, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The Netherlands will not take part in next year’s Eurovision Song Contest after public broadcaster NPO said there was “not enough support” for sending an act.

The decision reverses a previous U-turn after AVROTROS, the broadcasting company that is usually responsible for the Dutch entry, said it would boycott the contest for a second year in 2027 because of Israel’s continued participation.

NPO said last month it would make alternative arrangements to participate in the contest in the Bulgarian coastal city of Burgas next May.

But on Tuesday Jet de Ranitz, chair of NPO’s board of directors, said after holding talks with networks and staff that there was “not enough support” for a Dutch entry.

AVROTROS said in September it would be staying away until “transparent rules” were drawn up on countries involved in military conflicts to restore the “neutrality” of the event.

The Netherlands was one of five countries not to send an entry last year, but news broadcaster NOS still sent a team to cover the event and will do so again next year. Ireland has also said it will continue its boycott in 2027 and is not broadcasting the contest.

Staff critical

Around 500 NPO employees signed a letter a week ago criticising the broadcaster’s decision to look for a replacement for AVROTROS, saying that “the desire to take part in an entertainment programme is considered more important than the countless lives of people who are being murdered.”

De Ranitz did not directly mention Israel’s participation, but said NPO had concluded after consulting broadcasting licence holders that “it is too early at the moment to take part in the Eurovision Song Contest”.

“Because of the sensitivities around the issues that are taking place now, we have decided to step aside for now,” she said.

NPO is in charge of the Dutch broadcasting infrastructure, but programmes are made by autonomous licensed companies.

The European Broadcasting Union, which organises the song contest, said it regretted NPO’s decision. It said it recognised the “deep-rooted and genuine opinions about the song contest and that they vary strongly”, but argued the event was an opportunity to bring unity to a “divided world”.

Culture minister Rianne Letschert said NPO had made an “editorial decision” and it was not her place to intervene.

“The song contest is an event that touches many people and understandably gives rise to widely differing opinions,” she said. “I understand that none of the broadcasters are prepared to take over the entry for the song festival for 2027.”

item.title: “Significant minority” feel disadvantaged in Dutch society – SCP
item.description:
“Significant minority” feel disadvantaged in Dutch society – SCP

October 27, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

A “significant minority” of people in the Netherlands believe other groups in society gain an unfair advantage at their expense, according to a survey for the Dutch government’s social research agency SCP.

Around 30% of people say they feel disadvantaged in the housing market, while 28% believe their views are not properly represented in politics. A smaller group of around 7% thought the justice system was biased against them.

The report found that people with minority ethnic backgrounds and white Dutch people with non-academic qualifications were most likely to feel they were being treated unfairly.

“Dutch people who feel they have drawn the short straw are often in a less favourable position in the housing or labour market,” the report’s authors said.

“They are also more likely to be dealing with other disadvantages such as a lower income, a smaller network or poorer health.”

The SCP tracks people’s perceptions of whether they are fairly treated on issues such as housing, justice and observation of traditions on a monthly basis, using focus groups and surveys.

Traditions

The agency said there was evidence that both people with recent migrant backgrounds and white Dutch people were disadvantaged, but both tended to perceive that the other group was better off.

Native Dutch people felt that traditions such as Sinterklaas were being diluted in favour of festivals such as Eid al-Fitr, while recent migrants said there was almost no recognition of their traditions outside a few major population centres.

The lack of trust in institutions also influenced people’s voting behaviour, with those who felt disadvantaged more likely to support far-right parties such as the PVV and FVD.

The report said the majority of people did not feel disadvantaged, while around one in five people perceived themselves to be privileged over others. They were more likely to be university educated and vote for progressive parties such as D66 and Pro.

“In contrast to many graduates, people with vocational educations are more likely to see society as a place where groups compete with each other for scarce resources, attention and recognition,” the report said.

“Moreover, they are more likely to feel that their own group systematically gets more than other groups and place the responsibility for this mainly with the political system and the government.”

item.title: Dutch bitcoin broker Bitonic hacked, funds stolen
item.description:
Dutch bitcoin broker Bitonic hacked, funds stolen

October 27, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Dutch bitcoin broker Bitonic has been hacked and “small amounts” of cryptocurrency were stolen from customers, according to emails obtained by broadcaster NOS.

The hack took place on Sunday night, and all customers were immediately logged out of their accounts as a precaution. Bitonic says the vulnerability that led to the hack has since been fixed. Three customers lost money and have been fully compensated.

Other customer data could have been accessed during the attack, the company says, though there is no evidence of this yet.

Crypto stored offline on hard drive wallets, known as “cold storage”, remained unaffected.

Bitonic says it will closely monitor all transactions made online for the time being, potentially slowing down any trades.

The hack is the latest blow to the Dutch crypto market after a Rotterdam court declared Knaken, a Netherlands-based crypto platform, bankrupt in July. Prosecutors found that €7 million in customer funds had gone missing.
